title: MailMind
tagline: From 50 unread emails to inbox clear in about eight minutes.
summary: MailMind turns the passive, chronological inbox into an AI-orchestrated workspace: a Morning Brief, an inbox sorted by intent, AI-drafted replies you approve with one tap, a calendar, a chat assistant and hands-free voice triage. The AI does the heavy lifting; you always pull the trigger.

facts.label: Platform
facts.value: Desktop web app, dark and light themes

stats.label: core workspaces: Brief, Inbox, Drafts, Calendar, Voice
designed path from app open to inbox clear

sections.title: Background
text: MailMind is an AI-powered email application that treats the inbox as an active productivity hub instead of a passive list. I designed it end to end, from research and information architecture to a set of high-fidelity screens and an interactive prototype.
The central idea is simple: AI should do the sorting, summarising and first drafts, and a person should always make the final call.

sections.title: Challenge
text: How might we help someone clear a flooded inbox in minutes, while making sure they trust what the AI is doing on their behalf?
Most email tools bolt AI onto the same chronological list. The challenge was to rethink how the inbox is organised and to make every AI action visible, explainable and reversible.

sections.title: The Problem
text: Knowledge workers spend around 2.6 hours a day on email triage: reading, sorting and replying. Existing tools treat the inbox as a chronological dump, which keeps people in a reactive mode and mixes urgent client requests with newsletters.
Opening the inbox in the morning is the peak of the pain, and many people do not trust AI enough to let it send on their behalf.

bullets.title: For users
bullets.text: Morning anxiety, important emails buried in noise, constant switching between email and calendar, and repetitive replies.

bullets.title: For trust
bullets.text: Fear that an AI could send the wrong thing to a client, so full automation is a non-starter.

sections.title: Impact
text: What the design is built to change, before it is tested with real users:

bullets.title: Less morning anxiety
bullets.text: A three-sentence Morning Brief replaces a wall of unread items.

bullets.title: Faster triage
bullets.text: Emails are grouped by intent, so the user decides what to do instead of working out what each email is. The design targets up to 70% less triage time.

bullets.title: Trust by default
bullets.text: Every AI action is labelled and needs an explicit Approve or Edit before anything is sent.

bullets.title: Fewer context switches
bullets.text: Calendar, chat assistant and voice live inside the same workspace.

sections.title: Research Insights
text: I combined contextual inquiry, a survey and a competitive review of Gmail, Superhuman, Spark, Shortwave and others. Four insights shaped the product, and each one turned into a design decision.

bullets.title: Morning anxiety is the peak pain
bullets.text: Users dread opening the inbox at 9 AM and want a summary, not a list of 50 unread items. Design implication: a Morning Brief dashboard.

bullets.title: Distrust of full automation
bullets.text: Users want AI to do the heavy lifting, but they must pull the trigger. Design implication: strict human-in-the-loop validation.

bullets.title: Triage, not reading, is the time sink
bullets.text: Deciding what an email is takes more effort than reading it. Design implication: group by intent, not chronology.

bullets.title: Context-switching is costly
bullets.text: Replying often means finding a past invoice or checking a calendar. Design implication: calendar and an AI chat assistant inside the workspace.

sections.title: Personas
text: Two people anchored the decisions: one who needs speed, one who needs structure.

bullets.title: Sarah, the Startup Founder
bullets.text: Runs a 15-person startup and dreads mornings. Wants the inbox under 20 items by noon, never to miss an investor email, and replies drafted in under 10 seconds.

bullets.title: Marcus, the Enterprise Manager
bullets.text: Manages teams across three time zones and is CC'd on everything. Wants to delegate 40% of requests, see morning visibility into team comms, and track approvals without chasing.

sections.title: Design Process
text: I worked in five days, so I kept the process tight and front-loaded the thinking.

bullets.title: 1. Discover
bullets.text: Contextual inquiry, survey and competitive analysis to find the real pain.

bullets.title: 2. Define
bullets.text: A problem statement and Jobs-to-be-Done across functional, emotional and social needs.

bullets.title: 3. Structure
bullets.text: Hub-and-spoke information architecture and two core user flows.

bullets.title: 4. Wireframe
bullets.text: Lo-fi layouts for the dashboard, inbox and thread detail.

bullets.title: 5. Design
bullets.text: Hi-fi screens, states and a dark and light design system in Figma.

bullets.title: 6. Prototype and test next
bullets.text: An interactive prototype now exists. Next is testing it with real users.

sections.title: Jobs To Be Done
text: The problem statement: users need to triage a large inbox quickly and safely, but tools give them a passive list. I framed the needs as three kinds of jobs.

bullets.title: Functional
bullets.text: Sort 200+ emails into actionable categories within two minutes of waking up, draft replies without re-reading the thread, and cross-reference the calendar instantly.

bullets.title: Emotional
bullets.text: Feel in control of the overload, trust that nothing critical slips through, and end the day without inbox guilt.

bullets.title: Social
bullets.text: Appear responsive and professional, delegate without seeming dismissive, and keep a reputation for thoughtful replies.

sections.title: Information Architecture
text: MailMind departs from the flat inbox. It uses a hub-and-spoke model where the Morning Brief is the central hub, with specialised workspaces around it: Inbox, AI Drafts, Calendar and Compose, and Settings.

Content follows three tiers with progressive disclosure: the Brief as executive summary, then intent categories, then the full thread. The AI Chat Panel, Voice Mode and notifications cut across every screen.
captions: Sitemap: Morning Brief as the hub, with an adaptive sidebar and persistent AI chat

sections.title: User Flow Mapping
text: I mapped two journeys before drawing a screen. The primary flow is Morning Triage: open the app, read the three-sentence brief, work through intent segments, review AI drafts and reach inbox clear in about eight minutes.
The secondary flow is commute triage by voice: activate voice, listen to the brief, speak commands such as "reply" or "approve", and confirm through the same human-in-the-loop check.
captions: Morning triage and voice-driven commute triage

sections.title: Lo-fi Wireframes
text: I wireframed the three screens that carry the most weight: the dashboard, the inbox and the thread detail. Settling hierarchy in grayscale first meant colour and the AI accent could then be used purely for meaning.
captions: Dashboard, inbox view and thread detail wireframes

bullets.title: Human in the loop, always
bullets.text: An "AI suggests:" intent label sits on every AI action, and nothing is sent without Approve or Edit. This is the main trust mechanism.

bullets.title: Group by intent, not time
bullets.text: High Priority, General and Bulletins replace a single chronological list.

bullets.title: Summary before detail
bullets.text: The Morning Brief gives three sentences and urgency groups before any email is opened.

bullets.title: One workspace, no tab hopping
bullets.text: Calendar, compose and an AI chat panel stay beside the email, so context is never lost.

bullets.title: Hands-free when needed
bullets.text: Voice Mode is a distraction-free overlay for triage during commutes.

bullets.title: Quiet notifications
bullets.text: Alerts are grouped by urgency and non-urgent ones are silenced to protect deep work.

sections.title: Hi-Fi Design: Starting the day
text: The Morning Brief is the front door. A scannable widget gives a three-sentence summary of overnight activity, groups items by urgency and cross-references the calendar, so the first thing a user sees is a plan instead of a pile.
From there the inbox is segmented by intent: High Priority as assessed by AI, General threads and automated Bulletins. Opening a thread shows the full context with an AI-drafted reply ready to edit.
captions: Morning Brief: summary, urgency groups, calendar cross-reference
Thread detail with an AI-drafted reply

sections.title: Hi-Fi Design: Getting things done
text: The AI Drafts Queue is a horizontal card deck of generated replies. Each card carries an explicit intent label and a single-tap Approve, with Edit and Reject always in reach, and a toast confirms what just happened.
The AI Chat Panel handles the questions that normally mean several tabs and searches. A user can ask for something like "find the invoice draft" and get the answer without leaving the thread.
captions: AI Drafts Queue: intent-labelled cards with Approve, Edit and Reject
AI Chat Panel for cross-referencing past context

sections.title: Hi-Fi Design: Scheduling and voice
text: Calendar and Compose is a synchronised split-screen. Dragging an email onto a slot schedules it and fills in a smart reply that confirms the time, so scheduling no longer means switching apps.

Voice Mode is an immersive, distraction-free overlay for hands-free triage. The assistant reads the brief aloud, accepts commands such as reply or approve, and still asks for confirmation before anything is sent.
captions: Calendar and Compose: drag an email to schedule it

sections.title: Design System: Calm Command
text: The interface follows a dark-first system I called Calm Command. Neutral surfaces keep the screen quiet, and a purple gradient is reserved for AI, so anything AI-generated is recognisable at a glance. Type pairs Neue Haas Grotesk with Inter, icons use Phosphor, and colours and spacing are tokens so dark and light themes stay in sync.

sections.title: Outcome
text: The result is a complete product concept: a researched problem, a hub-and-spoke architecture, five connected workspaces, a reusable design system and an interactive prototype of the full flow.
The design is ready to be tested with real users, starting with how much they trust the AI drafts and how quickly they reach inbox clear.

bullets.title: Usability testing
bullets.text: Time the morning triage flow with first-time users and measure the real reduction against the 70% target.

bullets.title: Trust calibration
bullets.text: Test how much explanation the "AI suggests:" label needs before people approve without re-reading.

bullets.title: Delegation workflows
bullets.text: Serve Marcus's need to hand requests to teammates and track approvals.

bullets.title: Accessibility
bullets.text: Audit contrast across both themes and add a full keyboard path for Voice Mode actions.
